lesson.title: 22.4 Liters: The Molar Volume of a Gas at STP
lesson.summary: Molar volume is the volume occupied by one mole of any ideal gas under a specified temperature and pressure, and at the standard conditions of 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atm it equals 22.4 liters for every gas.
lesson.body:
Avogadro's law established that equal volumes of gas, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of moles, regardless of what gas it is. A direct consequence is that one mole of any ideal gas, at any fixed temperature and pressure, occupies the same volume as one mole of any other ideal gas at those same conditions. That shared volume is called the molar volume, and it is one of the most useful shortcut numbers in all of gas chemistry, because it means you never have to solve PV = nRT from scratch for a gas at standard conditions; you can just multiply or divide by a fixed number.

Standard temperature and pressure, abbreviated STP, is traditionally defined as 0 degrees Celsius (273 K) and 1 atm. You can derive the molar volume at STP directly from the ideal gas law by solving for V with n = 1 mol: V = nRT/P = (1 mol)(0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))(273 K) / (1 atm). Multiplying the numerator: 0.0821 times 273 is 22.4. Dividing by 1 atm changes nothing. So V = 22.4 L, which is the molar volume of any ideal gas at STP. It is worth pointing out that this is the same 22.4 L/mol used as a known value back in the gas stoichiometry and ideal gas constant chapters; here you have finally seen where that number actually comes from.

One important note on terminology: this 0 degrees Celsius, 1 atm definition of STP, giving 22.4 L/mol, is the traditional one still used in most introductory courses and is the one used consistently throughout this unit. IUPAC has since updated the formal definition of STP to 0 degrees Celsius and 1 bar (which is very slightly less than 1 atm), and under that newer definition the molar volume works out to about 22.7 L/mol instead. The two numbers are not interchangeable, so always check which STP convention a problem is using; every calculation in this unit uses the 1 atm, 22.4 L/mol convention.

Molar volume makes simple conversions fast. Suppose a balloon holds 5.60 L of helium gas at STP, and you want to know how many moles of helium that is. Instead of rearranging PV = nRT, just divide by the molar volume directly: n = V / 22.4 L/mol = 5.60 / 22.4 = 0.250 mol. That is a clean, exact answer, and it is exactly the same result you would get from the full ideal gas law, just reached in one step instead of four. This is the shortcut gas stoichiometry problems lean on whenever a reaction happens to occur at STP, letting you jump straight between moles of gas and liters of gas without ever explicitly writing out P, R, and T.
